Mark the start of a new chapter in this session.

Call this when the work shifts to a meaningfully different phase — e.g. after finishing exploration and starting implementation, after a fix lands and you move to verification, or when the user pivots to an unrelated request. The user sees a divider in the transcript and a floating table of contents for jumping between chapters.

Use sparingly: a chapter should cover a coherent stretch of work, not every tool call. A typical session has 3–8 chapters. Do not mark a chapter for the very first message — the session start is implicit.

The title is a short noun phrase ("Codebase exploration", "Auth bug fix", "Test verification"), not a sentence.

title.description: Short noun-phrase title for the chapter (under 40 chars). Shown in the table of contents.

summary.description: Optional one-line summary of what this chapter covers. Shown on hover in the table of contents.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__read_widget_context
tools.description: Read context from an embedded interactive widget. Widgets are rendered alongside chat from prior tool calls and can be interacted with by the user. Call this when you need to know the current state of a widget.

tool_name.description: The name of the widget tool to get context for

tools.name: mcp__ccd_turn__update_plan
tools.description:
Keep the task list the app shows under your latest message while you work. Every request that edits files or runs more than one command gets one (implement-and-test, investigate-then-fix, anything the user listed); only a single-command answer or pure conversation does not.

Never spend a message on this tool alone: send it IN THE SAME MESSAGE as another tool call (in parallel), so it costs no extra round trip.
- First call: with the VERY FIRST tool call of the turn, even one that only reads or lists files: {"items": [...]}, the whole plan in order, short imperative phrases (at most ~7 words, no numbering), the step you are starting "in_progress", the rest "pending". If you must look around first, make "Look at how X is set up" step one and refine the list once you know.
- Next step: {"advance": true} alongside the call that begins it (completes the in_progress step, starts the next pending one); after the last step, advance alongside wrap_up.
- Out of order: {"done": [2], "start": 4} (1-based).
- Plan changed, including right after the user interrupts or sends a new instruction mid-task: {"items": [...]} again, the new whole list, so the pinned list never shows an abandoned plan.
- Every {"items"} call says in "scope" what this request is to the session: "first_task" (nothing finished here yet); after that, "new_task" (unrelated work: it builds on nothing done, found or decided here) or "continuation" (everything else: anything a few tool calls settle, the next iteration, acting on what you just investigated or suggested, even if that work gets its own commit or PR; when unsure, this one). A "new_task" turn opens with a start_session offer and reaches this call only if the user chose Do it here.
Keep exactly one step in_progress while working and none when everything is done. Do not also write the plan as a numbered list in your message: the pinned list is the plan.

scope.description: Required with items: "first_task", "continuation" or "new_task" (see the tool description). Omit on advance / done / start updates.

session.description: When you delegated this step to a session you started: that session's short name (from start_session's result). The app shows its live state on the step.

items.description: The whole plan, in order (1–12 steps); replaces the previous list.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_turn__wrap_up
tools.description:
Fill the "next step" box the app shows at the end of your turn: a two-or-three-sentence recap and, when this turn leaves the user a decision to make or a step to take, one question and buttons that answer it; a turn with nothing pending ends with the recap alone, and the app then draws no box. Call it once in EVERY turn in which you kept a task list, changed files, ran commands, or completed multi-step work: when this turn's work is done, before any closing message (it also checks off the task list; no closing update_plan is needed). Skip it for short answers, pure conversation, or a brief read-and-explain turn — a reply that names a follow-up is not brief: ask or propose it, and call this.

Your closing message is ordinary text right after this call, the last thing you say this turn: your answer to the user in full, which the recap never replaces. Never write it before this call, where it can reach the user cut to a short summary. The result says whether the box shows your question: ask in the message only a question it does not show.

Fields (write recap last) — ask and recap are said to the user, in the second person; a reply button's label is the user's words back to you:
- ask (with actions, only when the next move is the user's call — a choice of approach, a go-ahead to fix, commit, push, post or send, an approval): just that ONE decision in one short sentence, never two joined by "and" ("Which fix first?"), with no reason or recommendation and without listing the options the buttons give: your pick, actions[0], is drawn as the primary button. At most 100 characters.
- recap: what is now true or changed, then where it stands, including what is not done or not verified (for example: nothing committed, or not checked in the app). Two or three short sentences, about 40 words / 300 characters, in the project's own words. No recommendation here.
Every field is a top-level parameter holding plain prose (actions: a JSON array); none contains markup or another field.

ask.description: The one question (≤100 chars) when the next move is the user's call — a choice, a go-ahead (to act here on what this turn found, say), an approval: the decision alone, with no reason or recommendation and without listing the options the buttons give (actions[0] is your pick). Like the recap, never point at anything else in the conversation. Omit it, and actions, when nothing waits on the user.

blocked.description: true when your work stops here until the user answers (the app marks the session as waiting on them); omit when the answer can wait.

action.description: An app action update_plan's result listed as available, or one your own work this turn made available; others are refused, and one that later stops being available is dropped (as actions[0], with your ask and other answers), so do not guess. Offer commit, create_pr or verify only once the work the user asked for is done, not every turn. Omit for a reply.

label.description: For a reply: the button text, 1–3 words (4 only when three cannot say it) / 24 characters — "Yes, fix 1", "Not now": a button, not a sentence. A click sends it to you as the user's answer. Never a go-ahead to commit: that is the commit app action. No leading / or !. Ignored for an app action.

actions.description: 1–2 buttons, recommendation first. They are answers to your ask: the first accepts your recommendation, and another is there only when it is a realistic alternative the user might pick instead — not a menu of everything you mentioned. When blocked is true, they are the most likely answers to your question. While Auto-fix is on for the session's PR, none offers to watch it, fix CI, resolve conflicts or address comments. Never repeat an offer the user passed over, as an app action, a reply or a question in your closing message, unless what it acts on has changed since or they bring it up.

recap.description: Two or three short sentences to the user (≤300 chars): what is now true or changed, then where it stands, including what is not done or not verified. Its first sentence is the sidebar status. It must stand on its own, since it is also read away from the transcript and the box draws under anything you write after this call: never point at anything else in the conversation ("listed below", "see above", "in my message").

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__browser_batch
tools.description: Execute a sequence of Browser pane tool calls in ONE round trip. Each item is {name, input} where input is exactly what you'd pass to that tool standalone. Actions execute SEQUENTIALLY (not in parallel) and stop on the first error. Use this tool extensively to quickly execute work whenever you can predict two or more steps ahead — e.g. navigate, click a field, type, press Return, screenshot. Each tool's own permission check runs per item — a step on a site the user hasn't allowed either asks the user inline (and continues if they allow) or is refused, which stops the batch; if a step is refused for a missing permission, call that tool on its own (that call can ask the user), then batch the rest. Screenshots and other images are returned interleaved with outputs; coordinates you write in THIS batch refer to the screenshot taken BEFORE this call. browser_batch cannot be nested, and preview_start is not batchable — but if the Browser pane isn't open yet, a batch whose FIRST action is navigate with a url opens it (other actions still need an open page).

name.description: Tool name (e.g. computer, navigate, find, form_input, read_page). browser_batch cannot be nested. A tabs_create's new tabId is only returned when the batch ends — load that tab in a later call.

input.description: That tool's input — same shape you'd pass when calling it directly. For computer items whose action is left_click, right_click, double_click, triple_click, left_click_drag, key or type, and for form_input items, include action_summary in the item's input, as you would when calling that tool directly.

actions.description: List of tool calls to execute sequentially. Example: [{"name":"computer","input":{"action":"left_click","ref":"ref_12"}},{"name":"computer","input":{"action":"type","text":"hello"}},{"name":"computer","input":{"action":"screenshot"}}]

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
tools.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

action.description:
The action to perform:
* `left_click`: Click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `right_click`: Click the right mouse button at the specified coordinates to open context menus.
* `double_click`: Double-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `triple_click`: Triple-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `type`: Type a string of text.
* `screenshot`: Take a screenshot of the screen.
* `wait`: Wait for a specified number of seconds.
* `scroll`: Scroll up, down, left, or right at the specified coordinates.
* `key`: Press a specific keyboard key.
* `left_click_drag`: Drag from start_coordinate to coordinate.
* `zoom`: Take a screenshot of a specific region for closer inspection.
* `scroll_to`: Scroll an element into view using its element reference ID from read_page or find tools.
* `hover`: Move the mouse cursor to the specified coordinates or element without clicking. Useful for revealing tooltips, dropdown menus, or triggering hover states.

coordinate.description: (x, y): The x (pixels from the left edge) and y (pixels from the top edge) coordinates. Required for `left_click`, `right_click`, `double_click`, `triple_click`, and `scroll`. For `left_click_drag`, this is the end position.

text.description: The text to type (for `type` action) or the key(s) to press (for `key` action). For `key` action: Provide space-separated keys (e.g., "Backspace Backspace Delete"). Supports keyboard shortcuts using the platform's modifier key (use "cmd" on Mac, "ctrl" on Windows/Linux, e.g., "cmd+a" or "ctrl+a" for select all). Page zoom shortcuts (e.g. "cmd+=", "ctrl+-", "cmd+0") are not supported - use the `zoom` action to magnify a region of the page instead.

duration.description: The number of seconds to wait. Required for `wait`. Maximum 10 seconds.

scroll_direction.description: The direction to scroll. Required for `scroll`.

scroll_amount.description: The number of scroll wheel ticks. Optional for `scroll`, defaults to 3.

region.description: (x0, y0, x1, y1): The rectangular region to capture for `zoom`. Coordinates define a rectangle from top-left (x0, y0) to bottom-right (x1, y1) in pixels from the viewport origin. Required for `zoom` action. Useful for inspecting small UI elements like icons, buttons, or text.

scale.description: For `screenshot` and `zoom` only. Scale factor in [0.1, 1] for the returned image; 1 (default) uses the full image token budget, 0.5 returns an image at half the width and height (~quarter of the tokens). Coordinates are ALWAYS in the full-resolution coordinate frame (reported with every scaled screenshot), never in the scaled image's own pixels.

repeat.description: Number of times to repeat the key sequence. Only applicable for `key` action. Must be a positive integer between 1 and 100. Default is 1. Useful for navigation tasks like pressing arrow keys multiple times.

ref.description: Element reference ID from read_page or find tools (e.g., "ref_1", "ref_2"). Required for `scroll_to` action. Can be used as alternative to `coordinate` for click actions.

modifiers.description: Modifier keys for click actions. Supports: "ctrl", "shift", "alt", "cmd" (or "meta"), "win" (or "windows"). Can be combined with "+" (e.g., "ctrl+shift", "cmd+alt"). Optional.

action_summary.description: A few words saying what this action does on the page and to what, for example 'Sends the drafted reply to pat@example.com' or 'Opens the Filters menu'. Set it on every left_click, right_click, double_click, triple_click, left_click_drag, key and type action. State the effect only, and accurately: no reasons, nothing about what you were asked or allowed to do, no passwords or other secrets.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__find
tools.description: Search the current page in the Browser pane for elements whose accessibility-tree line (role / name / text) contains `query`, case-insensitively. Returns up to 20 `ref_N` matches usable with `computer`/`form_input`.

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

query.description: Text to look for in an element's role, name or text (case-insensitive substring, e.g. "Sign in", "search", "Add to cart").

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__form_input
tools.description: Set the value of a form element identified by `ref` (from read_page/find). Handles input/textarea/select/checkbox/contenteditable.

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

ref.description: Element reference ID from the read_page tool (e.g., "ref_1", "ref_2")

value.description: The value to set. For checkboxes use boolean, for selects use option value or text, for other inputs use appropriate string/number

action_summary.description: A few words saying what this form fill does on the page and to what, for example 'Sets the delivery date to 29 September'. State the effect only, and accurately: no reasons, nothing about what you were asked or allowed to do, no passwords or other secrets.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__get_page_text
tools.description: Extract the visible text of the Browser pane's page (article/main content first, falls back to body innerText).

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__javascript_tool
tools.description: Execute JavaScript in the Browser pane's page for DEBUGGING and INSPECTION only. Do NOT use this to implement UI changes — edit source code instead.

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

action.description: Action to perform (only `javascript_exec` is supported).

text.description: The JavaScript code to execute. Evaluated in the page context with REPL semantics: top-level `await` works, and the result of the last expression is returned automatically — write the expression you want (e.g. `window.myData.value`, or `await fetch(url).then(r=>r.json())`) rather than `return ...`. Return values are serialized as JSON.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__navigate
tools.description: Navigate the Browser pane to a URL, or go "back"/"forward" in history. If the Browser pane isn't open yet, this opens it at the URL (no dev server needed).

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

url.description: The URL to navigate to. Can be provided with or without protocol (defaults to https://). Use "forward" to go forward in history or "back" to go back in history.

force.description: If the page shows a "Leave site?" dialog because of unsaved changes, discard those changes and navigate anyway. Defaults to false.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__preview_list
tools.description: List servers started with preview_start. Returns serverIds for use with other preview_* tools.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__preview_logs
tools.description: Get server stdout/stderr output. Use to check for build errors, verify server behavior, or read debug output. Use 'level' to filter to errors only, or 'search' to filter for specific text. Use after preview_start.

level.description: Filter by level: 'all' (default) shows all output, 'error' shows only lines containing error/exception/failed/fatal

search.description: Filter to lines containing this text (e.g., '[DEBUG]', 'POST /api')

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__preview_start

url.description: URL to open in the Browser pane without a dev server (instead of starting one by `name`).

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__preview_stop
tools.description: Stop a server started with preview_start.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__read_console_messages
tools.description: Get console output (log, info, warn, error, debug) from the Browser pane.

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__read_network_requests
tools.description: List network requests, or fetch a specific response body by `requestId`.

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

urlPattern.description: Substring filter on the request URL as listed (auth values show as REDACTED).

requestId.description: If provided, returns the response body for this request instead of listing.

limit.description: Max entries to return when listing (default: 50).

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__read_page
tools.description: Read the current page in the Browser pane as a YAML-style accessibility tree. Each interactive element is tagged `[ref_N]` for use with `computer`/`form_input`/`find`. Prefer this over screenshot for verifying text and structure. Output is limited to 50000 characters by default; if it exceeds the limit it is truncated with a note — pass a larger max_chars, or use ref_id/depth to focus.

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

filter.description: 'interactive' returns only clickable/typable elements; 'all' (default) returns the full tree.

ref_id.description: Restrict the tree to descendants of this `ref_N` (from a previous read_page).

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__resize_window
tools.description: Emulate a viewport size in the Browser pane tab. Presets: mobile (375x812), tablet (768x1024), or desktop, which clears the size emulation and returns the tab to the pane's own responsive size. Custom sizes need both width and height. An emulated size applies to that tab across reloads and navigation (scaled down to fit when it is larger than the pane): reset it with preset "desktop" as soon as you finish testing. The desktop app may also clear a size you set when your turn ends, so set it again in a later turn if you still need it. A size the user picked from the pane's own Viewport menu is theirs and stays until they or you change it; leave it unless they ask. colorScheme (light/dark) emulates prefers-color-scheme on that tab; it survives reloads and preset "desktop" does not touch it, but the pane re-syncs the tab to the app's light/dark theme when that theme changes or the pane reopens; local documents and static HTML previews always render light. The mobile preset (and any width < 768) also emulates a mobile device: Android Chrome user agent and 5 touch points, so pages detect a touch phone; your clicks still arrive as mouse clicks. Reload the page after switching so load-time device gates re-run.

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__tabs_close
tools.description: Close one Browser pane tab. Closing the last tab closes the Browser pane itself (reopen it with `preview_start`).

tabId.description: Tab to close.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__tabs_context
tools.description: List every Browser pane tab (origin only — titles are page-authored). Returns {browserOpen, tabs: [{tabId, origin, isActive}]} plus a line saying whether the pane is currently displayed or hidden (a hidden pane still works, but its page runs as a background page, so timing and performance numbers from it can be off; prefer `read_page` / `get_page_text` over screenshots while it is hidden). browserOpen is false (and tabs empty) until `preview_start` or `navigate` opens the pane, so you don't need to call this before opening it.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__tabs_create
tools.description: Open a fresh blank Browser pane tab; returns the new tabId. Opens in the background by default — set `foreground: true` when the user wants to watch. Prefer `preview_start` with a `url` when you know the destination; use `navigate` to load a URL into a blank tab.

foreground.description: Front the new tab (user asked to see it or is following along). Default false: open behind the user's current tab.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__tabs_select
tools.description: Front the given Browser pane tab. Background tabs keep running while you drive them, so front one only when the user should look — or for a page that pauses itself while hidden (e.g. a video player).

tabId.description: Tab to front.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Code_iOS_Simulator__control
tools.description: Run, test, and visually verify iOS apps in the iOS Simulator on this Mac. Use this whenever the user wants to see or try their iOS app ("run my app", "test this on iPhone", "does this look right?", "try the new screen"), not only when they mention the simulator by name. Simulator only: this tool cannot drive or stream a physical iPhone or iPad. If the user wants the app on their real device ("on my iPhone", "on my device"), build and deploy for the device with your normal build tools instead, and say the live panel only shows simulators. 'attach' opens a live panel so the user can watch. When the user wants to see the app, call 'attach' FIRST, before building: it is cheap, opens instantly on a booted simulator, and boots one that is off, so do not boot a simulator yourself. 'launch' installs and launches a built .app. Build it first, with the user's own build tooling or this server's 'build' tool when this session has it; launch re-attaches on its own, but do not rely on that instead of the early attach. Screenshots and tap/swipe/text verification are headless and need no panel. Don't open the panel when the user only asked to build/compile or to run unit tests. Coordinates are in device points (origin top-left); the 'launch' result reports the device's point dimensions.

action.description: What to do. 'attach' opens the live simulator panel for the user. Call it BEFORE you build or launch, as soon as the user wants to see the app: on a booted simulator it opens immediately, and it boots one that is off and returns while that one is still starting up. Do not skip the early attach because 'launch' also attaches: the panel should be open before the build starts. The panel is the user's view, not a precondition: 'screenshot' and input actions work without it. Skip it only when the user has no interest in watching; 'launch' installs and launches an .app (it also re-attaches, but call 'attach' early rather than relying on that); 'screenshot' returns a PNG of the current screen; 'tap'/'swipe'/'text'/'button' inject input; 'press_key' presses a hardware key 'count' times: return, delete (backspace), an arrow, select_all, undo or redo; 'set_appearance' switches the device to light or dark mode; 'appearance' says which it is in; 'set_keyboard' shows or hides the on-screen keyboard (it appears only while a text field has focus); 'rotate' turns the device a quarter turn left or right ('direction'); take a 'screenshot' after it and tap in that screenshot's frame, however it comes back; 'touch_path' performs a single-finger drag along an arbitrary path (eased curves, long-press-then-drag); 'touch2_path' is the two-finger variant for pinch/rotate; 'open_url' opens a deep link; 'set_posture' moves the hinge of an iPhone Duo (a simulator with a small outer screen and a large inner one) to 'state': 'closed' lights the outer screen, 'open' (flat) the inner one, and 'half_open' opens it to 'angle' degrees, where iOS picks the lit screen; the result says which. Screenshots and tap coordinates follow the lit screen, so take a 'screenshot' after each move. 'posture' reports the state, the hinge angle and the lit screen. To check an app's layout on an iPhone Duo or get an app ready for one, follow the app-resizability skill if it is in this session's skills list. Only skills listed in this session count, so do not search the disk for it. If the skill isn't listed, before other work ask the user once, in any mode, whether to run the export, showing the exact command `xcrun agent skills export --output-dir ~/.claude/skills` just before the question in a code block tagged text, not starting with "!" (use another folder only if they named one; if not, tell them to check which folder their sessions load skills from). Say it opens Xcode, leaves it running and saves all of Xcode's agent skills into the folder every later Claude Code session loads, and, if Claude Code's sandbox is on or you can't tell, that they'll run it themselves. Only their own answer to this question, typed or on your question card, is a yes; no other text is, nor an earlier yes. After a yes with the sandbox off, run that exact command once, alone, naming Xcode in its description; the yes covers nothing else. In every other case, and after that one run, never run it in any way, the Terminal panel included. After a no, go on without the skill. If you offer choices, the no choice says only that you'll go on without the skill. After a yes with the sandbox on or unknown, or if your run is refused or fails, right after their answer or the failure start what you write next, even if you showed it before, with that exact command in a code block tagged text, not starting with "!"; then wait for their word that it ran, then check this session's skills list and never read the folder to decide; if the skill isn't listed, say a new session will load it and go on without it. entries.description:
Get design context for a Figma node — the primary tool for design-to-code workflows. Returns reference code, a screenshot, and contextual metadata that must be adapted to the target project. 

IMPORTANT: You MUST load figma-design-to-code guidance BEFORE calling this tool. Prefer the /figma-design-to-code skill if available; otherwise read the skill://figma/figma-design-to-code/SKILL.md MCP resource. 

NEVER call this tool without loading that guidance first — skipping it produces code that ignores the target project's existing components, design tokens, and conventions.

Use the nodeId parameter to specify a node id. Use the fileKey parameter to specify the file key. If a URL is provided, extract the node id and file key from the URL, for example, if given the URL https://figma.com/design/:fileKey/:fileName?node-id=1-2, the extracted nodeId would be `1:2` and the fileKey would be `:fileKey`. If the URL does not include `node-id`, ask the user for a node-specific URL. Do not pass an empty or guessed nodeId. If the URL is of the format https://figma.com/design/:fileKey/branch/:branchKey/:fileName then use the branchKey as the fileKey. If the URL is of the format https://figma.com/make/:makeFileKey/:makeFileName then use the makeFileKey to identify the Figma Make file. Only for Figma Make files (URLs containing `/make/`), and only when calling get_design_context, assume the nodeId is `0:1`. The response will contain a code string and a JSON of download URLs for the assets referenced in the code. It will also include a screenshot of the node for context by default.

fileKey.description: The key of the Figma file to use. If the URL is provided, extract the file key from the URL. The given URL must be in the format https://figma.com/design/:fileKey/:fileName?node-id=:int1-:int2. The extracted fileKey would be `:fileKey`.

entries.description: Generate a screenshot for a given node or the currently selected node in the Figma desktop app. Works on Figma design files (URL path `/design/`), FigJam boards (`/board/`), and Figma Slides (`/slides/`). The optional `maxDimension` parameter (positive integer, max 65536, default 1024) caps the longer edge of the rendered PNG in pixels — increase it when you need to inspect fine detail, decrease it for thumbnails or to save context. content.text: Figma is read, and the codebase exploration is still finishing. While it does, I have three structural questions that change the plan.

questions.question: How should a case study be structured in the router? This affects the side nav, the snap-scroll 'hump', and the overview buttons that jump to sections.

options.label: One page, CSS scroll-snap (Recommended)
options.description: One route per case study. Overview, Deep dive, Walkthrough and Gallery are full-viewport sections with scroll-snap. The side nav tracks the active section and the overview buttons scroll to anchors. The 'hump' is a small resistance zone at the end of the deep dive. Simplest, and the URL hash can deep-link to sections.

options.label: Separate routes per section
options.description: /projects/ping, /projects/ping/deep-dive and so on, with animated transitions between them. Cleaner isolation, but the 'scroll past the end to snap to the next section' feel is harder to build and needs custom wheel handling.

questions.question: What should the home page URL look like when a case study icon is selected?

options.label: Query/path per project (Recommended)
options.description: e.g. /projects/ping. Selecting an icon updates the URL, so previews are shareable and Back works. The start page lives at /.

options.label: Local state only
options.description: Icon switching doesn't touch the URL. Simpler, but previews can't be linked to.

questions.question: When should the start page greet visitors?

options.label: Every visit to / (Recommended)
options.description: The start page is the root route, and Enter/Start goes to the home page. No storage, predictable, and easy to share.

options.label: First visit only
options.description: Remember in localStorage and send returning visitors straight to the home page. It adds state and a redirect, and you can't re-view the start page easily.

<result># Internal Transit: repo map for the redesign

Repo root: `/Users/trounceabout/Repos/Personal/internal-transit` (branch `main`, clean apart from untracked `.claude/`, `.entire/` and `cody-pixel-portrait-transparent.svg`).

## Surprises that change the plan

1. **There is no top nav or header component.** The commit "drop old nav" (7171ec6) removed it. `BaseLayout.astro` still has `pt-16` on `<body>` and an unused `activeNav?: "work" | "blog"` prop. Each page carries its own "Home" breadcrumb. See §3.
2. **There is no clock, date widget or moon/sun icon toggle.** The theme toggle is a text button in the footer. See §3.
3. **"Undercurrent" is not this site's design system.** It is the name of one case study. It has a scoped, demo-only token set, `--uc-demo-*`, in `src/styles/undercurrent-demo.css`. The site's own tokens are `--portfolio-*` in `global.css`, plus shadcn's Button. There is no "Undercurrent" package. See §4.
4. **There are no tests** (no vitest, playwright or stories) and **no CLAUDE.md**. The only conventions doc is `README.md`.
5. **The dot-grid is CSS-only.** It is a `::after` pseudo-element in `ProjectLayout.astro`, not a component.
6. `astro.config.mjs` has `site: "https://codykeisler.me"`, while the README says internaltransit.com.

## 1. Framework, tooling, routing

- **Astro 6** (`astro ^6.0.8`) with `@astrojs/react` (React 19 islands), `@astrojs/mdx` and `@astrojs/vercel` (adapter). `@sentry/astro` is also configured, and `@astrojs/rss` is installed.
- **Tailwind v4** is used as a Vite plugin (`@tailwindcss/vite`). There is no `tailwind.config`. Config lives in `src/styles/global.css` via `@theme inline`.
- **Package manager:** bun (`bun.lock`). The README says `bun install` and `bun run dev`. Node must be `>=22.12.0`.
- **Experimental flag:** `queuedRendering: { enabled: true }`.
- **Routing is Astro file-based**, in `src/pages/`. Dynamic routes use `getStaticPaths()` over content collections:
  - `src/pages/index.astro`: `/`
  - `src/pages/projects/[slug].astro`: `/projects/<id>`
  - `src/pages/blog/index.astro`: `/blog`
  - `src/pages/blog/[slug].astro`: `/blog/<id>`
  - `src/pages/rss.xml.js`: `/rss.xml`
  - `src/pages/api/subscribe.ts`: `POST /api/subscribe`, a Buttondown proxy
- **Alias:** `@/*` maps to `./src/*` (tsconfig).
- **Content collections** are in `src/content.config.ts` (glob loaders):
  - `blog`: `src/content/blog/*.md(x)`
  - `projects`: `src/content/projects/*.mdx`
- **Motion:** yes, `motion ^12.42.2` is installed.
  - `src/lib/animations.ts` uses `animate, stagger` from `"motion"` (vanilla).
  - Several React islands use `motion/react`: `UndercurrentSandbox`, `ThemeRevealSandbox`, `DocsViewerSandbox`, `TerminalConversation`, `useStreamingReveal`, `useTypewriter`.
- **Other deps:**
  - Icons: `pixelarticons` (primary), `@hugeicons/*` (blog and home Writing only), `lucide-react` (demo islands only).

questions.question: How should a case study be structured in the router? This affects the side nav, the snap-scroll 'hump', and the overview buttons that jump to sections.

options.label: One page, CSS scroll-snap (Recommended)
options.description: One route per case study. Overview, Deep dive, Walkthrough and Gallery are full-viewport sections with scroll-snap. The side nav tracks the active section and the overview buttons scroll to anchors. The 'hump' is a small resistance zone at the end of the deep dive. Simplest, and the URL hash can deep-link to sections.

options.label: Separate routes per section
options.description: /projects/ping, /projects/ping/deep-dive and so on, with animated transitions between them. Cleaner isolation, but the 'scroll past the end to snap to the next section' feel is harder to build and needs custom wheel handling.

questions.question: What should the home page URL look like when a case study icon is selected?

options.label: Query/path per project (Recommended)
options.description: e.g. /projects/ping. Selecting an icon updates the URL, so previews are shareable and Back works. The start page lives at /.

options.label: Local state only
options.description: Icon switching doesn't touch the URL. Simpler, but previews can't be linked to.

questions.question: When should the start page greet visitors?

options.label: Every visit to / (Recommended)
options.description: The start page is the root route, and Enter/Start goes to the home page. No storage, predictable, and easy to share.

options.label: First visit only
options.description: Remember in localStorage and send returning visitors straight to the home page. It adds state and a redirect, and you can't re-view the start page easily.

input.content:
# Portfolio redesign (v2.0): plan

## Context
Full top-to-bottom redesign of the portfolio (Astro 6 + React 19 islands + Tailwind v4, bun). Figma section "redesign" (file `yQsyiiyNzkw04y8TR6UCcK`, node `37:4587`) has these frames: Welcome (start), Home - Library, Case study - Ping (+ nav-on-scroll variant), Sub-nav, About, and a "New buttons" section. Goal: a guided, presentation-style experience with a persistent top nav (with live clock) and bottom action bar, keyboard shortcuts, and an About page.

## Findings that change the brief (please sanity-check)
1. **Astro, not a React SPA.** Routing is file-based (`src/pages`). Case studies are MDX in `src/content/projects/*.mdx`, rendered by `src/layouts/ProjectLayout.astro`.
2. **No top nav, clock, or icon theme toggle exists.** The theme toggle is a text button in `Footer.astro`. Theme = `.dark` class on `<html>` + `localStorage.theme`, with a view-transition sweep (reuse this logic).
3. **"Undercurrent" is not this repo's design system** (it's a case study with a scoped `--uc-demo-*` kit). The site's real tokens are `--portfolio-*` in `src/styles/global.css` (bg/ink/muted/accent, `--media-frame-shadow`, radii). **Plan assumption: extend `--portfolio-*` tokens in `global.css`** (light + dark come free). `ui/button.tsx` (shadcn) is unused; the real button is `PillButton.astro`.
4. Motion (`motion` ^12) is already installed and used (`src/lib/animations.ts`). No tests, no CLAUDE.md.
5. Figma variables are not bound (empty), so exact values come from design context/screenshots when building each piece. Button section specs (`64:5974`) get pulled at implementation time.

## Architecture decisions
- **Keep Astro. Use `ClientRouter` (view transitions)** so the persistent top nav and bottom nav don't flash between routes. Interactive pieces are React islands or small vanilla scripts. (Large decision: confirm.)
- **Routes** (decided with you):
  - `/` = Start page (every visit)
  - `/projects/[slug]` = home preview for that project; `/projects` redirects to the first. Switching icons updates the URL via a React island using `history.pushState`.
  - `/projects/[slug]/` case-study content lives on one page with scroll-snap sections (below).
  - `/about`
  - Open question for build time: whether the home preview and case-study body are the same route (preview = first snap section, "Open project" scrolls/snap to Deep dive) or two routes. **Recommended: same route**, the Overview *is* the home preview, so icon bar -> overview, "Open project" -> next section. (Matches "Overview buttons take the user to the marked section".)
- **Shortcuts**: one small `src/lib/shortcuts.ts` registry; bottom nav renders actions from a per-page config; each action = label, key glyph, handler. Ignore when focus is in inputs or with modifier keys.
- **Button press feel**: `:active { transform: scale(.97) }` plus shadow reduction (offset shadow collapses toward 0 to feel "pressed"), using existing `--media-frame-shadow`-style tokens, not Figma's. Respect `prefers-reduced-motion`. Use `motion` `press` only if CSS isn't enough.

## Phases (my suggested order differs slightly: foundation and cleanup first)
Each phase is a small, lintable, committable change. Phase 0-1 are the riskiest (touch the layout shell and delete content).

**Phase 0: Remove articles (⚠️ deletes files)**
Delete `src/pages/blog/*`, `src/layouts/BlogLayout.astro`, `src/content/blog/`, `src/pages/rss.xml.js`, `src/lib/categoryConfig.ts`, the `blog` collection in `src/content.config.ts`, category tokens in `global.css`, RSS link + `activeNav` in `BaseLayout.astro`, the "Writing" block in `index.astro`, and unused deps (`@astrojs/rss`, `@hugeicons/*`). Decide separately: orphaned `SubscribeForm.tsx` + `api/subscribe.ts` (recommend remove for now). Update README mentions.

**Phase 1: Foundation**
- Tokens (`global.css`): secondary button surface/ink/shadow, key-cap glyph chip, nav item states, pressed state. Both themes.
- `Button` secondary (extend `PillButton.astro` or a new `ActionButton.astro`), with key glyph slot, default / hover-focus / pressed / disabled states per Figma "New buttons".
- `TopNav.astro`: Projects / About (active state), live date-time (small script, `Intl.DateTimeFormat`, updates each minute, user's local time), GitHub / Discord / LinkedIn icons, sun/moon icon theme toggle (reuse existing view-transition toggle logic from `Footer.astro`). Remove `Footer.astro` and the `pt-16` hack.
- `BottomNav.astro` + `shortcuts.ts`. Hidden on Start and About.
- Enable `ClientRouter` in `BaseLayout`; make scripts safe across `astro:page-load`.

**Phase 2: Start page (`/`)**
Centered hero ("Hi there / I'm *Cody* [avatar]", Design Engineer / Rock Hill, SC / Version 2.0, social icons, Start button with Enter). `Enter` -> `/projects/ping` (first project). Reuse `/me-big-head-only.svg` and Redaction font. No top/bottom nav.

**Phase 3: Home / project preview**
- Icon bar (large icon buttons: Ping, Undercurrent, Watchtower, plus a disabled "Coming soon" tile as in Figma), selected one enlarged. Horizontal scroll with the selected item scrolled into view on small screens.
- Preview: "Project Ping" label, big Redaction headline with accent phrase (from `tagline`/`accentPhrase`), description, Type / Accessories / Role / Scope meta rows (extend project frontmatter: `type`, `accessories`).
- Motion: subtle entrance (fade/translate stagger, `motion` `animate`/`stagger`), cross-fade between projects, icon bar slide/scale. Basic first, polish after.
- Bottom nav actions: **Open project (Enter)**, **Watch walkthrough (W)**, **Back (Esc)** per Figma.

**Phase 4: Case study format (⚠️ largest change)**
- `ProjectLayout.astro` -> snap container (`scroll-snap-type: y proximity/mandatory`), sections: **Overview**, **Deep dive**, **Walkthrough**, **Gallery**. The "hump": a small overscroll/resistance zone at the end of the deep dive before snapping to the next section (CSS snap + an IntersectionObserver-driven short threshold; avoid hijacking wheel events unless proximity snapping can't deliver the feel; prototype this first).

When something needs interactivity — a newsletter signup form, a toggle, a dialog — React drops in as an island via `@astrojs/react`. shadcn provides accessible, unstyled-first components that are copied into the project (not imported from a package), so there's no library lock-in and the code is fully under my control.

# Internal Transit

My personal home on the internet. Lives at [internaltransit.com](https://internaltransit.com).

This is a portfolio site for my work as a product designer and design engineer, a blog that doubles as a newsletter, and eventually a podcast home. The point is full ownership — no platform middleman, no algorithmic feed, no dependency on a service that might disappear or change its terms. Everything here is mine.

---

## What it is

- **Portfolio** — case studies and work samples for product design and design engineering
- **Blog / newsletter** — writing that goes out as email to subscribers and lives permanently on the site
- **Podcast** — planned, not yet built

---


## Environment variables

Copy `.env.example` to `.env` and fill in the values. The file is git-ignored — never commit it.

| Variable             | Where to get it                                                                   |
| -------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `BUTTONDOWN_API_KEY` | Buttondown account settings → API                                                 |
| `SENTRY_DSN`         | Sentry project settings → Client Keys (DSN)                                       |
| `SENTRY_AUTH_TOKEN`  | Sentry account settings → Auth Tokens (used for source map uploads at build time) |

/
├── public/              # Static assets served as-is (favicon, images)
├── src/
│   ├── assets/          # Assets processed by Astro (optimized images, etc.)
│   ├── components/      # Astro and React components
│   ├── content/         # MDX content collections (blog posts, work)
│   ├── layouts/         # Page layout wrappers
│   ├── lib/             # Utility functions and helpers
│   ├── pages/           # File-based routing (each file = a route)
# Copy this file to .env and fill in your values.
# Never commit .env to git — it's already in .gitignore.

# Get this from your Buttondown account settings → API
BUTTONDOWN_API_KEY=

# Get this from your Sentry project settings → Client Keys (DSN).
# SENTRY_DSN is used server-side (Node/SSR). PUBLIC_SENTRY_DSN is the same
# value but prefixed PUBLIC_ so Astro exposes it to the browser bundle.
SENTRY_DSN=
PUBLIC_SENTRY_DSN=

# Get this from your Sentry account settings → Auth Tokens (needed for source maps)
SENTRY_AUTH_TOKEN=

# Get this from your pixelarticons.com purchase confirmation email or Gumroad library.
# Run `bun run icons:upgrade` after setting this to unlock the full 4,400+ icon
# set locally — without it, only the free 564-icon tier installs. This is a
# manual, explicit step (not a postinstall hook) so third-party code with
# network access doesn't execute unattended on every install; Vercel runs the
# same command explicitly as part of its configured Install Command.
PIXELARTICONS_LICENSE_KEY=

content.content:
**[shadcn/ui](https://ui.shadcn.com) + React 19 islands**
Most of the site is static Astro components. When something needs interactivity — a toggle, a dialog — React drops in as an island via `@astrojs/react`. shadcn provides accessible, unstyled-first components that are copied into the project (not imported from a package), so there's no library lock-in and the code is fully under my control.

**[Vercel](https://vercel.com)**
Astro has an official Vercel adapter and the deployment integration is seamless — push to `main`, site updates. Preview deployments per PR make it easy to review changes before they go live. No server config to manage.

**[Sentry](https://sentry.io)**

- @astrojs/rss
- @hugeicons/core-free-icons
- @hugeicons/react

content.text:
Phase 0 is finished on a new branch, `feat/remove-articles`. Nothing is committed yet. Lint, the build, and Prettier on the files I touched all pass. I haven't loaded the site in a browser.

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
- Deleting a feature in Astro means unwinding a *chain*: the pages depended on a layout, which depended on a helper (`categoryConfig`), which depended on CSS tokens, which depended on a content collection. I traced those references with grep first so nothing was left dangling.
- Astro generates pages from content collections, so removing the `blog` collection also removed the blog routes from the build. The build now produces only the home page and the three case studies.
- Two things were already broken before my changes. `astro check` reports 2 errors in the Sentry config (`dataCollection`). Prettier also flags 17 older files, mostly the Watchtower demo. I left both alone.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

**What changed** (17 files, about 780 lines removed):
- **Deleted:**
  - the blog pages and `BlogLayout`
  - the only post
  - the RSS feed
  - `categoryConfig.ts`
  - the newsletter form and its `/api/subscribe` route
- **Edited:**
  - the home page no longer has a "Writing" section
  - `BaseLayout` lost the RSS link and an unused prop, and its default description no longer mentions writing
  - the `blog` collection and 16 category color tokens came out of `global.css`
  - `ProjectLayout` and `README` no longer mention the blog
  - the Buttondown key came out of `.env.example`
- **Dependencies removed:** `@astrojs/rss` and both Hugeicons packages.

Do you want me to commit Phase 0 and then start Phase 1, or review the diff first?

content.text:
Phase 1 is built and checked in the browser, in both themes. Nothing is committed yet.

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
- **Shortcuts work by finding buttons, not registering handlers.** A button declares `data-shortcut="esc"`, and one global listener finds that element on the current page and clicks it. Pages only declare buttons, and the listener keeps working across navigations with no re-binding.
- **`transition:persist` only works on a real element.** On an Astro component it silently did nothing: the header was rebuilt on every navigation and the clock came back blank. Putting it on the `<header>` inside `TopNav` fixed that.
- **Client-side navigation breaks scripts that run once.** Astro swaps the page body without a reload, so scripts that cached elements at load stopped working. I fixed the fade-in, the dot-grid reveal, and the Lightbox by re-running them on `astro:page-load`. The theme is also re-applied after each swap.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

**What's in place:**
- **`ActionButton`**: the secondary button, with a key-cap tile (Enter, Esc, or a letter).
  - It is transparent at rest, and on hover it fills with ink and uses the existing `--media-frame-shadow`.
  - On press it shrinks to 97% and the shadow collapses.
  - Reduced motion is respected.
- **`TopNav`**:
  - Projects/About, with the current page in bold.
  - A moon icon in dark mode and a sun in light.
  - A live local date and time (24-hour, like `Nov 27 16:16`).
  - GitHub, Discord and LinkedIn icons.
  - The header persists across pages.
- **`BottomNav`**: a fixed bar built from each page's `actions`. The case-study pages currently get "Back (Esc)", and Esc navigated home without a page reload.
- **Removed:** the old `Footer`. Its theme-toggle logic moved to `src/lib/theme.ts`.
- **New tokens** in `global.css`: key-cap tint, nav-active tint, and a pressed-button shadow.

**Things to know:**
- ⚠️ **The Discord link is a placeholder** (`https://discord.com/`) in `src/data/links.ts`. Send me the real one and I'll swap it in.
- The "Projects" nav item points to `/` for now. It will move to the new home route in Phase 3.
- I read "Nov 24 11:37" in Figma as 24-hour time. Say so if you'd prefer 12-hour with AM/PM.
- I couldn't force the pressed state, so the shrink and shadow change are untested. Hover and the filled look matched Figma.
- I added a local `.claude/launch.json` for the dev server. It's untracked, so I'll leave it out of the commit.

Do you want me to commit Phase 1, or review the changes first?

I started a new branch, `feat/start-page`, so this phase doesn't pile onto `feat/remove-articles`. `★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────` - **The portrait SVG is single-color.** It uses `fill="currentColor"`, so an `` always paints it black, which disappears on the dark background. I draw it as a CSS mask over an ink-colored box, so it's cream in dark mode and near-black in light mode, like the Figma frame. - **Navigation works across the start page.** Pressing Enter went from `/` to `/home` with no reload. The top nav, which the start page hides, appeared with its clock already running. That's the persisted header from Phase 1 doing its job. - **The fade-in waits for JavaScript.** The page content starts invisible and fades in once the script loads. That felt slow on first load in the dev server, and I'll check it against the production build when we polish. `─────────────────────────────────────────────────` **What changed:** - **Start page at `/`:** it matches the Figma Welcome frame ("Hi there / I'm *Cody* [portrait]", the Design Engineer / Rock Hill, SC / Version 2.0 line, the three social icons, and a pill Start button with the Enter key-cap). It has no top or bottom nav. On phones the three facts stack vertically. - **`/home`:** the current project list moved here temporarily, so nothing is orphaned before Phase 3 replaces it. The top nav's "Projects" link, the Back (Esc) action, and the breadcrumb Home link now point there. - **Shared `SocialLinks` component:** the top nav and the start page both use it, and About will too. - **Moved your portrait:** I moved the untracked `cody-pixel-portrait-transparent.svg` from the repo root into `public/` so the site can serve it. - **Still open:** the Discord link is still a placeholder. content.text:
Phase 3 is built and checked in the browser, and nothing is committed yet. I started a new branch, `feat/home-preview`, on top of `feat/start-page`.

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
- **I dropped the React island from the plan.** I'd planned a React island with `pushState`, but Astro's client-side router already does this. Each project is a real page at `/home/<slug>`, and the icon bar is marked `transition:persist`, so the same bar element survives each click. That's what lets CSS animate the old tile shrinking and the new one growing. Browser Back and Forward also work, and no state code is needed.
- **A tiny script covers the one thing a persisted bar can't do itself.** It reads the URL, moves `aria-current` to the right tile, and slides the bar so that tile is centered. It's the same pattern as the top nav's active state.
- **The slow-looking fade-in was the pane, not the code.** Screenshots caught elements mid-fade because the preview pane throttles animations while idle. The elements were fully opaque once measured.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

**What's in place:**
- **Icon bar:** a selected tile at 124px in the project color, 70px tinted tiles for the rest, and a "Coming soon" tile. It slides horizontally on small screens.
- **Preview:** project name, a large headline with the accent phrase in the project color, the description, and Type / Accessories / Role / Scope rows. The preview text fades up in sequence each time you switch.
- **Bottom actions:** Open project (Enter, filled), Watch walkthrough (W), and Back (Esc, to the start page). Walkthrough only appears for projects with a video.
- **Smaller changes:**
  - a `featured` look on `ActionButton`
  - a new `type` field in project frontmatter
  - the clock now hides on phones so the social icons fit

**Please check:**
- ⚠️ **I guessed the Type values:** Ping "Redesign", Undercurrent "Design system", Watchtower "Redesign". Tell me the right ones.
- **The old project list is gone.** I'll recreate its row style for the About work history in Phase 5, from git history.
- **Open project and Watch walkthrough still link to the old case-study page.** Phase 4 builds the real destination and the `#walkthrough` section.
- **Phone layout:** the three bottom actions stack and overlap the page text. That's on the list for the Phase 6 small-screen pass.

Do you want me to commit Phase 3 on `feat/home-preview`, or review the changes first?

Our hosting management app had a persistent awareness problem: users could tell that something had happened, but not always what it meant, whether it mattered, or what to do next. I led a redesign of the notification experience to make account activity clearer, more actionable, and easier to trust. Rather than treating notifications as isolated alerts, I reframed them as part of a broader activity system and designed a dedicated inbox experience around that model.
## The problem The existing experience used a familiar bell-and-popover pattern, but it wasn't a good fit for the system underneath it. Our "notifications" were actually built on top of a decade-old account activity model with inconsistent structure, vague messaging, and unpredictable content length. A single item might contain a simple server update or a few paragraphs of technical maintenance details. The UI looked modern, but the experience was hard to scan and difficult to act on. That left users asking themselves questions like what had happened? Is this still in progress? What is it related to? Do I need to do anything? And most importantly: **Where do I go next?**
## The approach A year earlier, I had tried to modernize the experience by adapting it to that more standard notification pattern. That approach didn't hold up, because the real problem wasn't visual polish, it was the underlying product model. The system wasn't built around lightweight alerts. It was built around events and account activity. Once I stopped trying to force it into a conventional notification UI, the right direction became much clearer. Instead of designing a better popover, I designed around the structure the product already had.
## The solution I redesigned the experience as a full-page destination with two connected views, an inbox for unread and relevant events and a full account history. This gave users a clearer place to check what was new, while also giving the system enough room to show meaningful detail and history.
The original popover constrained both the content and the mental model. Moving the experience into a dedicated inbox created more room, clearer hierarchy, and a stronger sense of place in the product.
The system was built around notifications containing multiple updates over time, but the old interface flattened that structure. Reframing each notification as a timeline of events made the interface more understandable because it reflected the actual logic of the system.
The old experience surfaced information, but didn't do much to help users respond. Introducing dynamic actions based on the latest event state reduced the work users had to do after interpreting a message and made the system more useful in the moment.

Embracing the structure of the underlying system instead of fighting it was key.

Rather than flattening account activity into generic alerts, I used that event-based model to create a clearer mental model for users, shifting the experience from passive information display toward guided problem-solving.

This reinforced an important lesson for me: familiar UI patterns only work when they match the logic of the system behind them.

The strongest part of this work wasn't the interface itself, it was reframing the problem. Once I treated notifications as activity rather than alerts, the product direction became much more coherent.

Most of the frontend experience was implemented, but release was paused due to backend dependencies and shifting team priorities.

<style>
  /* MDX content comes from a separately-compiled component tree (rendered via
     <Content /> in [slug].astro), so Astro's default *scoped* styles never
     attach to it — every rule here needs :global() or it silently does nothing. */
  /* Two separate spacing tokens, easy to conflate but serving different
     jobs:
       --ping-section-gap   — vertical rhythm BETWEEN sections. Stays a
                               fixed 60px at every viewport width — this is
                               breathing room in the reading flow, not
                               something that should compress on mobile.
       --ping-card-padding   — the INSET inside a bordered/gradient card
                               (Problem/Approach/Solution) and the
                               <article> wrapper's own horizontal margin.
                               This one DOES scale down on narrow screens
                               (24px mobile / 40px tablet / 60px desktop,
                               matching <article>'s own
                               px-6 sm:px-10 lg:px-[60px]) — a flat 60px
                               inset squished the readable column badly on
                               phones. Collapsing both into one variable
                               previously made the inter-section gap shrink
                               along with the card padding, which read as
                               sections crowding each other on mobile. */
  .article-body {
    --ping-section-gap: 3.75rem; /* 60px, fixed at every width */
    --ping-card-padding: 1.5rem; /* 24px */
  }

  @media (min-width: 40rem) {
    .article-body {
      --ping-card-padding: 2.5rem; /* 40px */
    }
  }

  @media (min-width: 64rem) {
    .article-body {
      --ping-card-padding: 3.75rem; /* 60px */
    }
  }

  /* Each top-level block in the MDX body is wrapped in its own
     `.ping-section`, so this gap can sit on both sides of a section as
     real padding (padding needs a real box on each edge — a
     margin-collapse-via-adjacency-selector approach only works for a flat
     list of siblings, and margin between siblings COLLAPSES rather than
     stacking, which reads as inconsistent spacing once some sections also
     have their own border/background — a card's edge should have a
     definite, non-collapsing gap around it). The first section only gets
     bottom padding, matching Figma's Intro frame using pb-[60px] instead
     of py-[60px] since there's nothing above it to pad against.
     Problem/Approach/Solution below add their own padding-LEFT/RIGHT only
     (not the `padding` shorthand) — the shorthand would overwrite this
     rule's padding-top/-bottom outright, since both rules have equal
     specificity and the later one wins on every side it touches. Setting
     only the two horizontal longhands here means their own left/right
     inset composes with (rather than replaces) this rule's vertical gap. */
  .article-body :global(.ping-section) {
    padding-top: var(--ping-section-gap);
    padding-bottom: var(--ping-section-gap);
  }

  .article-body :global(.ping-section:first-child) {
    padding-top: 0;
  }

  /* "The problem" gets a plain 1px stroke outline and its own left/right
     inset (on top of the padding-top/-bottom every section already has
     from the rule above) — the one section styled as a bordered card
     rather than a plain full-bleed block. padding-top/-bottom here
     re-declare --ping-section-gap (the FIXED token), not
     --ping-card-padding (the responsive one) — using the responsive
     variable for the vertical sides was the exact bug this replaced:
     it made this section's vertical gap shrink along with its horizontal
     inset on mobile, instead of staying fixed like every other section's. */
  .article-body :global(.ping-section--problem) {
    border: 1px solid var(--section-border-color);
    border-radius: 0.75rem; /* 12px */
    padding-top: var(--ping-section-gap);
    padding-bottom: var(--ping-section-gap);
    padding-left: var(--ping-card-padding);
    padding-right: var(--ping-card-padding);
    margin-top: var(--ping-card-padding);
    margin-bottom: var(--ping-card-padding);
  }

  /* "The approach" gets the same left/right inset, matching "The problem"
     above — vertical padding stays on the fixed --ping-section-gap for
     the same reason. position: relative gives the ::after grid layer
     below a containing block to size itself against. Unlike "The problem",
     this section stays borderless/full-bleed on purpose — the border is
     what marks Problem as the one "card" section, and adding one here
     would blur that distinction. No overflow: hidden here (unlike the
     original version of this rule) — the ::after grid layer below is
     deliberately wider than this section's own box (it bleeds 40px past
     the left/right edges), and clipping at the section boundary would
     hide exactly that bleed. The page-level overflow-x-hidden on <body>
     (BaseLayout.astro) is what stops that bleed from ever causing a
     horizontal scrollbar on narrow viewports. */
  .article-body :global(.ping-section--approach) {
    position: relative;
    padding-top: var(--ping-section-gap);
    padding-bottom: var(--ping-section-gap);
    padding-left: var(--ping-card-padding);
    padding-right: var(--ping-card-padding);
  }

  /* Decorative dot-grid background for "The approach". A single tiled
     radial-gradient draws a 1px dot every 24px using the same weak
     --section-border-color hairline already used for "The problem"'s
     outline, so it reads as part of this design system rather than a
     borrowed effect. (An earlier version of this used a two-axis
     repeating-linear-gradient line grid, matching aphera.co's reference;
     swapped to dots after finding a closer reference. A per-project
     accent-color tint was also tried and reverted — read as too loud/
     colorful for this background texture even at 25% strength; the
     neutral hairline color works better.)
     Deliberately ::after, not ::before: generated content always paints
     after an element's real children by spec, so ::after guarantees this
     stays behind the section's images/copy without depending on z-index
     stacking order against the LightboxImage markup (which has its own
     position: relative wrapper). The negative z-index below is
     belt-and-suspenders on top of that. Also inert to pointer/click
     interaction. Starts fully transparent — observeGridReveal()
     (src/lib/animations.ts) adds .grid-active via IntersectionObserver
     once the section scrolls into view, which is what actually plays the
     gridSequence fade (defined in global.css). */
  .article-body :global(.ping-section--approach::after) {
    content: "";
    position: absolute;
    /* Bleeds the grid 40px past the section's own left/right edges (top/bottom
       stay flush) so it reads as wider than the text column above it, similar
       to aphera.co's reference. This section has no overflow: hidden of its
       own (unlike "The problem"/"The solution") specifically so this bleed
       isn't clipped — the page-level overflow-x-hidden on <body>
       (BaseLayout.astro) is what stops it from ever causing a horizontal
       scrollbar on narrow viewports instead. */
    inset: 0 -40px;
    /* "1px, transparent 1px" (not "0, transparent 1px") is what makes a
       crisp dot instead of a soft blurred blob — the color stays solid from
       center out to the 1px radius, then cuts hard to transparent at that
       same radius. */
    background-image: radial-gradient(
      circle,
      var(--section-border-color) 1px,
      transparent 1px
    );
    background-size: 24px 24px;
    /* Fades the grid out near all four edges instead of cutting off hard
       — two gradients (one per axis) multiplied together via
       mask-composite: intersect, so a point only stays fully opaque where
       BOTH the horizontal and vertical fade are opaque (i.e. away from
       every edge at once). -webkit- variants are Safari's still-required
       prefixed equivalents (mask-composite ergo is broadly supported
       unprefixed now, but -webkit-mask-composite uses different keyword
       values, hence "source-in" there vs "intersect" above). */
    mask-image:
      linear-gradient(
        to right,
        transparent 0%,
        rgba(0, 0, 0, 1) 10%,
        rgba(0, 0, 0, 1) 90%,
        transparent 100%
      ),
      linear-gradient(
        to bottom,
        transparent 0%,
        rgba(0, 0, 0, 1) 10%,
        rgba(0, 0, 0, 1) 90%,
        transparent 100%
      );
    mask-composite: intersect;
    -webkit-mask-image:
      linear-gradient(
        to right,
        transparent 0%,
        rgba(0, 0, 0, 1) 10%,
        rgba(0, 0, 0, 1) 90%,
        transparent 100%
      ),
      linear-gradient(
        to bottom,
        transparent 0%,
        rgba(0, 0, 0, 1) 10%,
        rgba(0, 0, 0, 1) 90%,
        transparent 100%
      );
    -webkit-mask-composite: source-in;
    pointer-events: none;
    z-index: -1;
    opacity: 0;
  }

  .article-body :global(.ping-section--approach.grid-active::after) {
    animation: gridSequence 1.4s ease-out forwards;
  }

  /* "The solution" gets a translucent border and a subtle vertical-fade
     background, both tinted by the project's own --icon-color (set inline
     in the MDX, resolved the same way the headline accent and Postscript's
     divider already do) — so each case study gets a matching treatment in
     its own accent color instead of every project showing Ping's red.
     color-mix() against transparent is what lets a var()-sourced color
     carry a percentage opacity — CSS's plain `color / alpha%` syntax only
     accepts a literal color, not a custom property. */
  .article-body :global(.ping-section--solution) {
    border-radius: 0.75rem; /* 12px */
    padding-top: var(--ping-section-gap);
    padding-bottom: var(--ping-section-gap);
    padding-left: var(--ping-card-padding);
    padding-right: var(--ping-card-padding);
    margin-top: var(--ping-card-padding);
    margin-bottom: var(--ping-card-padding);
    border: 1px solid color-mix(in oklch, var(--icon-color) 50%, transparent);
    background: linear-gradient(
      0deg,
      color-mix(in oklch, var(--icon-color) 0%, transparent) 0%,
      color-mix(in oklch, var(--icon-color) 13%, transparent) 100%
    );
    background-origin: border-box;
    background-clip: padding-box, padding-box, border-box;
  }

  /* A heading still sits close to the content directly under it (16px),
     same as Figma's "The problem"/"The approach" heading+paragraph groups —
     this is intra-section spacing, unaffected by the section padding above. */
  .article-body :global(h2 + *) {
    margin-top: 1rem; /* 16px */
  }

  .article-body :global(h2) {
    font-family: var(--font-plex-sans);
    font-weight: 500;
    font-size: 1.5rem; /* 24px */
    line-height: 2.5rem; /* 40px */
    color: var(--portfolio-ink);
  }

  .article-body :global(p) {
    font-family: var(--font-plex-sans);
    font-size: 1.125rem; /* 18px */
    line-height: 2rem; /* 32px */
    font-weight: 300;
  }

  /* Paragraphs immediately following another paragraph (e.g. "The problem"'s
     three-paragraph run) sit tighter than the 40px inter-block gap above —
     Figma treats runs of body copy as one 16px-spaced group. */
  .article-body :global(p + p) {
    margin-top: 1rem; /* 16px */
  }

  /* Every `.ping-section` in Figma is a `flex flex-col gap-[40px]` —
     Intro's paragraphs vs. its image, Approach's copy vs. its two-image row,
     a Point's LabeledRow vs. its LoopVideo, all 40px apart regardless of
     element type. This is intra-section spacing between a section's direct
     children, distinct from `.ping-section`'s own 60px outer padding above.
     `:not(p)` keeps this from overriding the tighter 16px `p + p` run
     spacing below — a `p` following a `p` should stay at 16px, not jump to
     40px just because both happen to sit inside a `.ping-section`. */
  .article-body :global(.ping-section > * + *:not(p)) {
    margin-top: 2.5rem; /* 40px */
  }

  .article-body :global(a) {
    color: inherit;
    text-decoration: underline;
    text-decoration-skip-ink: none;
    text-underline-position: from-font;
  }
</style>

content.content:
Our product had grown through years of one-off decisions, uneven patterns, and design system false starts. The experience was functional, but it didn’t consistently feel like one product. Similar interface problems were being solved in different ways, foundations were incomplete, and the cost of maintaining consistency kept increasing as new work shipped. I helped grow Undercurrent into a more dependable shared system — one that could support day-to-day product work, improve consistency across surfaces, and create stronger foundations for bigger efforts like theming and dark mode.
Our existing server monitoring experience exposed very little of what customers actually needed to understand server health. The data we did show lacked context, important metrics were missing entirely, and there was no simple way to understand whether a server was healthy without already knowing how to interpret the numbers. I helped shape a new monitoring experience that made server health easier to understand at a glance, easier to investigate in detail, and easier to act on when something needed attention.
It also meant contributing across design and implementation.

The previous monitoring tab

The new direction

content.text:
Phase 4 is built and checked in the browser, and nothing is committed yet. I started a new branch, `feat/case-study`, on top of `feat/home-preview`. ⚠️ This is the largest change so far: it rewrites the case-study layout and reorders the content in all three project MDX files, so I'd review it before merging.

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
- **The hump works with plain CSS.** I measured it with real wheel input. A 3-tick nudge past the end of the Deep dive (about 295px) was pulled back. A 5-tick push (about 490px) crossed the halfway point and snapped to the Walkthrough. The threshold is about half a screen, and no wheel-event JavaScript is involved.
- **The page is data plus one MDX body.** Overview, Walkthrough, and Gallery come from frontmatter (`type`, `loomUrl`, and a new `gallery` list), and only the Deep dive is MDX. A reusable script restructured Undercurrent and Watchtower the same way as Ping.
- **A sticky header takes up space.** It made the page rest at `y=80` and look "scrolled" even at the top. Pulling the case study up by the header's height (`-mt-20`) gives the Overview a true `y=0` snap point.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

**What's in place:**
- **Overview:** a one-screen title slide with a springy icon tile, a headline whose words rise and de-blur in Motion, and the project facts.
- **Deep dive:** same write-up, now in a 900px column. The lead paragraph is larger, and Problem and Solution share one rounded card. Approach keeps its dot grid.
- **Walkthrough and Gallery:** the Loom video in a centered player, and a labeled grid of the existing stills and loops.
- **Side nav:** it tracks your scroll, and Deep dive expands into Intro / Problem / Solution / Approach / Examples / Postscript with tree lines.
- **Bottom actions:** Overview shows Deep dive (Enter), Walkthrough (W) and Gallery (G). Other sections show Next project (X). Back (Esc) is always there. I tested Enter, W, G, X and Esc.
- **Top nav:** it now hides on scroll down and returns on scroll up, on every page.

**Please check:**
- **Esc always goes back to the home preview**, even from deep inside a case study. Tell me if you'd rather it step back to the Overview first.
- **Undercurrent's gallery has only one image**, because it's mostly interactive demos. Say if you'd rather drop its Gallery section.
- **I wrote Gallery captions for Watchtower** ("Context and actionability" and so on). Please check the wording. I also fixed Watchtower's copy-pasted opener alt text.
- **Still open:**
  - The side nav is hidden below 1024px, with no mobile replacement yet.
  - The Overview is about 37px taller than a very short 768px window.
  - I couldn't judge the entrance animation's feel because the preview pane throttles animations, so please try it in your own browser.

Do you want me to commit Phase 4 on `feat/case-study`, or review the changes first?

content.text:
Phase 5 is built and checked in the browser, and nothing is committed yet. I started a new branch, `feat/about`, on top of `feat/case-study`. The page has no bottom nav, as you specified. The copy lives in `src/data/about.ts`, so you can edit it without touching layout code.

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
- **The work-history rows reuse the old home-list look.** The home list's badge square, hover fill rising from the bottom, and border change moved into a reusable `ProjectRow` component. Each row links to its case study, and a click navigated client-side with no reload.
- **The hero uses the same masking trick as the start page.** The portrait is a single-color SVG drawn as a mask over an ink-colored box, so it follows the theme. "Cody" gets the teal → blue → purple gradient by clipping a CSS gradient to its letters.
- **The About side nav tracks scrolling like the case-study one.** It has a bottom-of-page rule, so the short last section, "Elsewhere", still highlights when you reach the end.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

**What's in place:**
- **Hero and side nav:** a "Hi, I'm Cody" hero with the gradient name, and a sticky side nav (About me / How I work / Work history / Elsewhere) that highlights the section you're in.
- **Content sections:** the intro, quick facts (Role / Based in / Focus), the three numbered "How I work" principles, and Elsewhere pills for GitHub, Discord and LinkedIn.
- **Work history:** Nexcess and USC Aiken with their roles and dates, and Ping, Watchtower and Undercurrent as linked rows under the right roles.
- **Responsive and themes:** it works in both themes and at phone width with no horizontal overflow. On phones the side nav is hidden and the portrait wraps under the name.

**I need from you:**
- ⚠️ **The map SVG.** The "Based in" panel is a dot-grid stand-in. Send the SVG and I'll drop it in, or I can start exploring a real lo-fi dot-matrix map.
- **Company logos.** The Figma has logo tiles for Nexcess and USC Aiken, but I can't pull Figma images without downloading files. The tiles show a letter ("N", "U") for now. Send the SVGs and put the path in `src/data/about.ts`.
- **A reminder:** the Discord link is still a placeholder.

**Dev-server note:** midway, the preview server threw "Outdated Optimize Dep" errors and the page scripts stopped loading. Restarting it cleanly fixed that. If you ever see content stuck invisible in `bun run dev`, clear `node_modules/.vite` and restart.

Do you want me to commit Phase 5 on `feat/about`, or review the changes first?

content.text:
Phase 6 is built and checked in the browser at phone, tablet and desktop widths. The changes are on `feat/responsive`, stacked on `feat/about`, and are not committed yet. That finishes the six phases from the plan.

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
- **Unlayered CSS beats Tailwind utilities.** My new chip bar had its own `display: flex` in a component style block, which overrode Tailwind's `lg:hidden`. At 1024px both the side nav and the chip bar showed. The fix is to hide it in the same component's CSS with a media query. This is worth remembering for any component that sets `display` itself.
- **Key-caps mean nothing on a touchscreen.** They're now hidden when the device can't hover or the screen is narrow, which also saves about 36px per button.
- **Dev-server CSS goes stale after repeated edits.** It twice served an old compiled copy of a component's styles. A restart with `node_modules/.vite` cleared fixed it both times. That's a dev-only quirk and doesn't affect the production build.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

**What changed:**
- **Section chip bar:** below 1024px, the case study and About pages show a sticky row of section chips in place of the side nav. It slides up when the header hides, the current chip stays centered, and it works on both pages.
- **Bottom nav on phones:**
  - It's one row and never wraps, with a soft right-edge fade if it still overflows.
  - Home uses short labels ("Open", "Walkthrough"), and the case-study Overview uses "Video".
  - Type is a bit smaller.
- **About hero:** the "Hi, I'm Cody" line and portrait now stay on one line on phones.
- **Overview on short windows:** it has tighter padding on short laptop windows, so it fits a 768px-tall window.

**Known leftovers, for later polish:**
- Deep dive sub-items exist only on desktop. On phones you get the four top-level chips.
- The case-study Next project row is the tightest on a 375px phone but fits.
- The Discord link is still a placeholder.
- The map and company logos are still stand-ins until you send those assets.

Nothing is committed on this branch. When you want it committed, say so. The redesign stack is now `feat/remove-articles` → `feat/start-page` → `feat/home-preview` → `feat/case-study` → `feat/about` → `feat/responsive`. A PR from the last branch would carry everything. Want me to open one, or send the map and logos first?
